strengths: Novel staged-to-wild evaluation protocol addressing a genuine gap in fall detection research, with OOPS-Fall providing authentic real-world test scenarios
Systematic and rigorous benchmark construction following PRISMA guidelines with 8 public datasets unified under consistent 10-class taxonomy enabling multiple evaluation granularities
Well-motivated problem with clear healthcare significance and medically important distinction between fall events and persistent fallen states
Comprehensive experimental analysis with multiple frozen backbones, domain shift analysis via FVD and dimensionality reduction, and cross-subject/cross-view splits
Interesting empirical insights about generalization patterns: I3D's surprising robustness to in-the-wild scenarios despite modest in-distribution performance
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations (demographic bias, privacy concerns, surveillance risks) and suggestions for future work
Clear experimental setup with documented hyperparameters and promised code release supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant demographic bias in staged data: all datasets feature young, healthy subjects despite elderly being the target population, with no demographic impact analysis or cross-age domain adaptation experiments

Asymmetric staged-to-wild evaluation: staged data contains fine-grained 10-class labels while OOPS-Fall is only binary fall/no-fall, making it unclear whether performance gaps stem from domain shift or label granularity

Critical annotation quality concerns: re-annotation of 8 datasets with new 10-class taxonomy lacks inter-rater agreement metrics, inter-rater reliability, and validation of consistency across datasets; OOPS-Fall annotation procedure under-specified (number of annotators, agreement thresholds)

Limited problem-solving insights: paper identifies substantial generalization gaps (e.g., I3D binary fall sensitivity drops from 0.82-0.96 in-distribution to 0.68-0.82 on OOPS-Fall) but provides no domain adaptation baselines or fine-tuning experiments to address them

Incomplete experimental design: all methods use frozen pre-trained backbones without fine-tuning, no comparison to fall detection methods from literature, arbitrary dataset weighting cap (20x) lacks justification, simple temporal transformer (2 encoder blocks) may underperform

Insufficient analysis of domain shift factors: which specific shifts matter most (background, lighting, camera angle, subject age/health)? No fine-grained failure analysis or explanation for why I3D generalizes better beyond speculation about simpler feature spaces

Missing reproducibility details: code link placeholder in abstract ('OmniFall: Code:'), no discussion of OOPS-Fall license/availability, no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing (single run reported)
Cross-subject vs. cross-view fairness issue: training corpus significantly larger for cross-subject split, confounding architectural differences with data availability effects

strengths: Clinically motivated taxonomy distinguishing transient actions from static states, addressing the medically important insight that persistent fallen states are more critical than fall events
Rigorous systematic PRISMA-compliant dataset curation consolidating eight public datasets under consistent annotations, substantial organizational effort
Comprehensive domain shift analysis revealing dataset relationships and providing insights into why simpler backbones (I3D) generalize better than complex ones (VideoMAE) to out-of-distribution data
Novel staged-to-wild evaluation protocol with OOPS-Fall, the first rigorous cross-domain evaluation framework for fall detection
Multi-dimensional evaluation framework with cross-subject, cross-view, and segmentation tasks providing comprehensive generalization assessment
Thoughtful acknowledgment of limitations, privacy concerns, and societal impacts demonstrating awareness of real-world deployment challenges
Complete video segmentation labels enabling multiple evaluation granularities and frame-level analysis
weaknesses: OOPS-Fall curation critically underspecified: only 1.3k segments from 20,000 videos (6.5%), annotation procedure vague, no inter-annotator agreement reported, no documentation of action/demographic composition or representativeness analysis

Massive unaddressed domain gap: I3D sensitivity drops 40% (0.82→0.68), VideoMAE drops 73% (0.78→0.21), but paper provides diagnosis without solutions—no domain adaptation methods, augmentation strategies, or error analysis proposed despite this being essential for healthcare deployment
Annotation quality metrics absent: re-annotation of all staged datasets lacks inter-annotator agreement (IAA); OOPS-Fall annotation quality undocumented, undermining benchmark reliability

Demographic bias acknowledged but unmitigated: for elderly-targeted fall detection, the dominance of young subjects in controlled settings is fundamental, yet no age-stratified analysis, elderly subjects in OOPS-Fall, or demographic investigation provided

Insufficient OOPS-Fall analysis: no action distribution breakdown, subject demographics, environment characterization, or per-class domain gap analysis relative to staged data; lacks documentation depth of staged data

Limited problem-solving depth: identifies overfitting to staged distributions but provides no investigation of root causes, ablation studies of design choices (18 tokens, class weighting, temporal transformer architecture), or proposed solutions

Modest dataset scale: 14 hours of unique staged footage plus underspecified OOPS-Fall collection is relatively small by modern standards; paper does not discuss sufficiency for deep learning or compare to related domains

Frozen backbone limitation reduces practical impact: justification of frozen features for 'systematic comparison' is weak; fine-tuned models and domain adaptation would better leverage OOPS-Fall for improving real-world performance

Experimental rigor gaps: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or standard deviations; single runs reported; no confusion matrices or error analysis especially for OOPS-Fall; no sensitivity analysis to dataset inclusion/exclusion

Incomplete practical considerations: no inference latency analysis (critical for emergency response), occlusions identified but not analyzed, no real-time deployment evaluation, computational requirements unspecified
Dataset dominance not addressed: CMDFall and UP-Fall comprise 60% of staged data; no sensitivity analysis of conclusions to individual dataset inclusion
Missing validation protocol discussion: unclear whether OOPS-Fall is used for model selection, risking overfitting to this specific evaluation set

strengths: Addresses genuine field-wide problem: fragmented datasets with incompatible taxonomies and unknown real-world performance on staged fall detection systems

Significant data curation effort: unified 8 public datasets (~14h, 101 subjects, 29 camera views) under consistent 10-class taxonomy distinguishing transient actions from medically-critical fallen states
Novel staged-to-wild evaluation protocol: OOPS-Fall (1.3k segments from genuine accidents) enables first rigorous assessment of generalization from controlled to uncontrolled environments
Systematic methodology: PRISMA-compliant literature search with clear inclusion criteria; thoughtful re-annotation strategy; proper cross-subject and cross-view splits

Comprehensive experimental analysis: reveals non-obvious insights (e.g., I3D's simpler features generalize better OOD despite lower in-distribution accuracy) via FVD, feature visualization, and multiple backbones
Clear practical value: enables fair cross-dataset comparison previously impossible and establishes reference point for future fall detection research

Transparent discussion of limitations and societal impact: acknowledges demographic biases, privacy concerns, surveillance risks, and performance disparities, demonstrating thoughtfulness beyond technical contribution
weaknesses: OOPS-Fall annotation rigor insufficient: filtering procedure vague ('original tags' then 'manually verified'); no inter-annotator agreement reported; binary labels inconsistent with 10-class taxonomy for staged data; annotation protocol and number of annotators not specified—critical for benchmark credibility

Data availability and reproducibility unclear: 'Code:' appears incomplete in manuscript; dataset licensing, access procedures, and terms not explained; OOPS-Fall licensing status unknown; would be unfeasible to reproduce without supplementary details

Limited statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or variance estimates; single runs without multiple seeds; no significance testing—standard practice for benchmarks would report uncertainty bounds

Insufficient domain gap analysis: FVD and feature visualizations reveal gaps but don't decompose underlying factors (lighting? backgrounds? motion patterns? safety equipment?); missing root-cause analysis of why binary fall detection collapses on OOPS-Fall

No domain adaptation or transfer learning experiments: paper identifies the domain gap but only provides diagnosis, not treatment; even basic fine-tuning baselines or adaptation methods absent; purely observational contribution

Missing baseline comparisons: no published results from prior fall detection systems; unclear if performance is competitive on original datasets; makes it difficult to assess whether benchmarking is correctly configured

Segmentation results suggest formulation issues: MS-TCN++ achieves high frame accuracy (64.96%) but very low F1@50% (21.82%) on OOPS-Fall, indicating over-segmentation; limited discussion of whether temporal localization is appropriately framed for domain shift

Demographic and environmental limitations substantive: source datasets feature young, healthy subjects in controlled settings; limited relevance to elderly care (stated application); real-world OOPS-Fall may not fully address bias if sourced from non-representative accident videos

Cross-view evaluation incomplete: single-view datasets excluded from cross-view testing; OOPS-Fall only evaluated cross-subject, not cross-view; asymmetry not justified; reduces scope of generalization assessment
No exploration of fine-tuning: only frozen backbones tested; how fine-tuning affects generalization unknown; limits practical guidance for practitioners

strengths: Addresses a real problem: unifies 8 fragmented fall detection datasets with heterogeneous annotations under a standardized 16-class taxonomy with dense frame-level labels, enabling previously impossible cross-dataset comparisons
Significant annotation effort: 33 hours of densely annotated single-view footage (82 hours multi-view) with systematic quality assurance and team consensus processes

Novel evaluation protocol: introduces first rigorous staged→wild cross-domain benchmark enabling systematic assessment of real-world generalization, with test-only OF-ItW derived from genuine accidents

Well-designed synthetic data: OF-Synthetic demonstrates thoughtful methodology with systematic demographic control (age, ethnicity via OMB standards, Monk Skin Tone Scale, BMI), 30 fall mechanism types, and deterministic reproducibility
Comprehensive experimental analysis: domain shift via FVD/t-SNE/H-NNE, multiple training configurations, classification and segmentation tasks, cross-demographic evaluation (age, BMI)

Counter-intuitive empirical finding: OF-Synthetic alone achieves better OF-ItW performance (64.2% Fall F1) than OF-Staged (60.5-61.2%), suggesting controlled demographic diversity bridges domain gaps better than real staged diversity
Privacy-preserving approach: synthetic data reduces ethical concerns of collecting from vulnerable elderly populations
Strong reproducibility: clear methodology, promised dataset/code release, detailed appendix with splits, features, implementation details
Responsible disclosure: acknowledges limitations and societal impacts, discusses surveillance concerns and need for demographic reporting
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: purely a dataset/curation contribution with no novel methods; experiments use only frozen features + lightweight transformers, not state-of-the-art fine-tuning

Temporal mismatch in OF-Synthetic: median 2 segments/video vs. CMDFall's 116 (58× difference); synthetic videos focus on compact fall events while missing recovery phases (25% fall→floor→standup chains vs. 100% in staged)

Unresolved domain gap: best OF-ItW performance is 65.6% Fall F1 vs. 85.4% in-distribution CMDFall (19.8% gap); gap documented but not solved, and mechanism explaining synthetic>staged transfer not analyzed

Insufficient in-the-wild evaluation: OF-ItW is only 2.6 hours (vs. 14h staged, 17h synthetic), test-only protocol prevents domain adaptation studies, curated from OOPS dataset potentially inheriting biases, no analysis of missing accident types

Critical missing annotation quality metrics: inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ, IoU) not reported despite ~10 annotators; subjective decisions (fall-to-fallen transitions) not validated; two-pass QA specifics unclear

Inadequate fairness analysis: cross-age shows 13.2% sensitivity drop for toddlers, 9.7% for elderly; cross-BMI shows 10.7% drop for obese—these gaps reported but not analyzed for causes or mitigations, concerning given elderly deployment focus

Limited experimental scope: only three backbone networks tested; no comparison with specialized fall detection methods; no ablation studies on architecture or taxonomy design choices (why 16 classes?)

Synthetic data quality unvalidated: manual filtering of inappropriate content unclear; no quantitative metrics for temporal coherence or pose realism; generator biases (e.g., smiling while falling) suggest robustness issues
Weak statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single runs reported without seed specification; sample sizes for demographic splits not specified

Missing mechanistic insights: why does OF-Synthetic outperform OF-Staged? No failure case analysis, per-class performance for OF-ItW, or guidance on when to use which split; limited explanation of transfer learning mechanism

strengths: Addresses genuine problem of dataset fragmentation in fall detection with systematic PRISMA-compliant approach
Comprehensive benchmark construction: unified 16-class taxonomy, dense frame-level annotations, standardized cross-subject/cross-view splits enabling reproducible evaluation
Thoughtful synthetic data component with controlled demographic diversity (age, ethnicity, BMI) addressing both privacy concerns and data collection barriers
Rigorous multi-faceted domain analysis using Fréchet Video Distances, t-SNE/H-NNE visualizations, and feature clustering provides useful dataset similarity insights
Excellent documentation and reproducibility: detailed annotation procedures, split definitions, feature extraction specifications, and multi-view annotation strategy
Dual evaluation protocols supporting both classification and timeline segmentation tasks
Addresses real healthcare problem (fall detection for elderly) with clear societal motivation
weaknesses: Limited novelty for top-tier venue: primarily dataset aggregation and standardization without novel algorithms, methods, or theoretical contributions; uses entirely off-the-shelf models with no domain adaptation methods despite that being the core challenge

Severely poor cross-domain generalization undermines primary claim: best model achieves only 65.6% Fall F1 on wild test; single-source results range 20.5-64.2%, leaving no clear guidance for solving cross-domain transfer

Overstated synthetic data contribution: OF-Syn vs OF-Sta improvement is only 3-4 F1 points (likely noise); combined training yields only +1.4 F1 improvement over OF-Syn alone; missing ablations identifying which synthetic attributes help
Demographic generalization critically weak: -13.2% sensitivity drop for elderly subjects (most clinically relevant population), -9.7% for children; contradicts claim of addressing demographic biases
Test-only design of OF-In-the-Wild prevents domain adaptation research and standard benchmarking practices; only 2.6 hours of data (~3% of benchmark) with undisclosed OOPS dataset biases

Insufficient mechanistic analysis of domain gap: visualizations show separation but lack depth; no failure case analysis; Figure 8 temporal complexity discussion is superficial; weak timeline segmentation results (19.5%-28.6% F1@50 on wild) barely discussed
No inter-rater agreement metrics despite 10 annotators; only statement that 'team discussion established consensus' on difficult transitions is insufficient

Absence of critical experimental comparisons: no domain adaptation baselines (DANN, ADDA, etc.), no state-of-the-art fall detection methods, no self-supervised approaches, single backbone family limits generalization insights
Severe class imbalance (Fall 0.1%, Standing 24%) minimally addressed; large gap between accuracy and macro-F1 indicates imbalance affecting results significantly
Provides limited practical guidance: for practitioners, unclear whether to use staged/synthetic/combined data; weak wild results (20-65% F1) and lack of clear solutions undermine practical utility

strengths: Addresses genuine gaps in fall detection: fragmented datasets with incompatible taxonomies, staging bias, and ethical concerns about collecting from vulnerable populations
Comprehensive standardization: successfully unifies 8 public datasets under consistent 16-class taxonomy with rigorous cross-subject/cross-view splits following PRISMA guidelines
Novel in-the-wild component: first standardized benchmark for staged→wild generalization using genuine accident videos, enabling systematic OOD evaluation
Thoughtfully designed synthetic data: controlled demographic diversity (age, ethnicity, body type, skin tone via Monk Scale), deterministic generation for reproducibility, addresses privacy concerns

Comprehensive experimental validation: domain shift analysis across three feature types (I3D, VideoMAE, SigLIP2), classification with multiple configurations, timeline segmentation, cross-demographic splits

Interesting empirical finding: synthetic data alone (64.2% Fall F1) outperforms real staged superset (60.5-61.2%) on OF-ItW, suggesting controlled diversity may outweigh real footage—non-obvious insight
Excellent presentation: clear writing, well-motivated, detailed appendix with annotation procedures, prompt engineering, feature extraction specs; comprehensive supplementary material
Practical value: 16-class taxonomy distinguishes transient actions from persistent states, enabling detection of medically critical long-lie episodes even when fall event missed
weaknesses: Synthetic data quality concerns underexplored: lower temporal complexity (median 2 vs. 116 segments), required manual safety filtering for inappropriate content, acknowledged generator biases not characterized, quality beyond feature-space similarity not validated

Severe and persistent generalization gap: best model only 65.6% Fall F1 on OF-ItW, 'Fallen' state detection 41.0% F1; even in-distribution timeline segmentation caps at 73-78% F1@50, suggesting fundamental challenges beyond domain gap
Limited in-the-wild test set: only 2.6 hours (818 videos) curated from OOPS, test-only prevents internal validation, represents narrow slice of real falls, inter-annotator agreement not reported

Annotation quality not rigorously validated: ~10 annotators with consensus but no inter-annotator agreement metrics (κ, Fleiss' κ) reported; dense frame-level annotation error rates unknown; multi-view transfer strategy can propagate errors undetected

Demographic bias persists despite diversity claims: Figure 7 shows 13.2% sensitivity drop for toddlers, 9.7% for elderly when training on adults—OF-Syn demographic diversity insufficient to eliminate bias

Limited novel insights: experiments mostly confirm expected findings (domain gaps exist, diversity helps); no systematic investigation of why staged→wild transfer fails or which factors cause performance drops
Class imbalance not addressed: extreme label imbalance (Figure 2), macro-F1 consistently 20-40% lower than accuracy, no class reweighting or focal loss explored

Experimental design gaps: only VideoMAE-K400 for classification (no ResNet3D, SlowFast), feature extraction configuration varies substantially (Table 7) complicating cross-backbone comparison, no comparison with recent fall detection methods, only ASQuery for timeline segmentation
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or cross-validation on classification; unclear if synthetic vs. staged difference is statistically significant
Reproducibility concerns: Wan 2.2 model availability uncertain (recent arXiv), project URL not provided, code contingent on acceptance, mixing of CC-BY-NC-SA and MIT licenses may restrict use
